title: I found a way to let 3 AI models debate and stress-test my investment strategy
author: capibara13
selftext:
So a while ago I was rebalancing my portfolio and doing a deep dive into some detailed future predictions on society, AI, inventions, GDP growth, ROI on particular stocks, etc. Like many here, I used AI models for research, but I kept running into the same recurring issue: after double checking every thesis with 3 different AI models I got so tired of copy-pasting prompts back and forth between three browser tabs, that I started running an experiment: what if you could give 1 prompt about your thesis, and let the AI models take it from there and discuss it with each other to stress-test it?

I ended up building a simple platform around this concept, and I have used it for all my portfolio and investment decisions ever since. It saved me a lot of time (and money, I expect). I’d love to get this sub's perspective:  
  
\- Do any of you currently use a multi-model approach for strategy validation, earnings analysis, or thesis testing?  
\- When two models fundamentally disagree on a risk factor how do you decide who is right?  
\- For those analyzing filings and market trends: what kind of structure/prompting has given you the most objective counterarguments?   
\- Would a multi-AI platform such as Rauno be helpful to you for your investment strategy? You can try it out for free if you're interested in this workflow. I'll place the link in the comments.   
  
Curious to hear how you guys approach this!

comments.author: capibara13
comments.body: If people want to test this workflow for their investment strategy, then try it here: [https://rauno.ai](https://rauno.ai)

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Three models agreeing is much weaker evidence than it feels like. They train on overlapping data and they fail in correlated ways, so consensus mostly tells you the thesis is common, not that it is correct.

Where this would earn its keep is forcing each one to argue the opposite side and keeping the disagreements rather than the agreements. The disagreement is the part with information in it.

replies.author: capibara13
replies.body:
100% spot on about correlated errors. If three models trained on the same web data agree on a popular thesis, all it proves is that it's a mainstream consensus, not that it's correct.

That’s actually why the system in this case is set up to be adversarial rather than consensus-seeking: the AI models are explicitly instructed to argue the opposite side, so it's flagging anything that the other models say that it doesn't agree with. The real signal is entirely in the divergence. When Model A says "this is a structural moat" and Model B fires back with "no, it's a cyclical peak masked by temporary supply constraints," that friction is where the actual value lies.

Do you use a specific adversarial structure or persona (like assigning a dedicated short-seller thesis) when you research your investment strategy? Having the 3 varying perspectives is actually invaluable to me.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Adversarial helps, but only if the roles are assigned before the model sees the data. Hand all three the same context and then ask one to argue against it, and it mostly just picks holes in wording.

How are you seeding the disagreement?

replies.author: capibara13
replies.body:
In my experience with this setup, models actually do call each other out quite naturally when they disagree with a premise or an assumption. Rather than just echoing the previous point, they tend to evaluate the logic and push back with specific counterarguments.

To answer your question on how that disagreement is seeded: it primarily comes down to how the system prompt conditions the interaction. The system prompt explicitly frames the session as a fact-based debate where intellectual honesty and stress-testing take priority over consensus.

On top of that, you can add explicit adversarial instructions into the prompt (e.g. instructing a specific model to act as a dedicated short-seller or actively poke holes in the previous model's valuation metrics). That prevents the second and third models from just nitpicking semantics and forces them to target the underlying thesis.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
What that can't do is make any of them check the data underneath. They'll argue the thesis happily and all three still be wrong about the same bad series, because none of them ever priced a fill.

My own scorer paid 100 points for a number I'd invented and 55 for the true one. Adversarial prompting wouldn't have caught it.

replies.author: capibara13
replies.body:
Fair point on proprietary or completely invented figures: if you feed an LLM a fabricated number in a total vacuum, no amount of debate will magically summon the true ground truth.

That said, the 'garbage in, articulate garbage out' risk is why I added automatic web search to the models: directly after every user prompt, an autonomous live web search pulls fresh external data, earnings releases, or reporting directly back into the context window before the models respond.

So if a model hallucinates a stock price or leans on outdated data, the search retrieval corrects the counterparty with the actual reported numbers found online. It obviously doesn't turn an LLM into an order-execution engine, but having an automatic web search prevents them from just throwing narratives around incorrect statements.

Curious though: given that, do you keep LLMs completely out of your strategy or do you still find value in using them (like parsing earnings transcripts or predicting ROI)?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: web search fixes the stale number problem, not the invented one. three models reading the same earnings release will agree on it whether or not the market priced it in a week ago. the debate tells you the inputs are consistent, it doesn't tell you they're tradeable.

replies.author: capibara13
replies.body:
Yes generating short-term alpha or finding immediate arbitrage is not the specialty of the current frontier AI models. Next week's price action is heavily priced in.   
  
But a 3- to 5-year development (e.g., how hyperscaler capex constraints hit local power grids by 2028) cannot be fully priced in today. 

The real purpose here isn't trading signals, but deep thesis analysis: pitting bull and bear cases against each other, finding pros and cons, making an extensive risk-analysis, and long term predictions. That's where I think AI models can add value, especially when using multiple models.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: The 2028 grid thesis has the opposite problem though. Nothing scores it until 2028, so the debate can be wrong for three years and still read as insight the whole way. A short horizon at least tells you you were wrong by Friday. How are you planning to grade those calls before they resolve?

replies.author: capibara13
replies.body:
Ah yes, that’s the classic falsifiability problem with long-term investing. If the feedback loop is three years long, a very bad thesis can masquerade as deep insight the entire way down. I think the only way to prevent that is by forcing the debate to produce short-term, falsifiable signposts (leading indicators) rather than just arguing about the 2028 end-state. 

For the grid thesis, that means not waiting for 2028 earnings, but prompting the models to identify the canary in the coal mine over the next 2 to 4 quarters. If those intermediate milestones clearly miss, it means that the thesis is incorrect and you don't sit on dead capital for three years waiting for 2028 to prove you wrong.

Do you build explicit kill-criteria into your longer-horizon models, or are your systems purely mechanical on short-term price/volume?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Signposts help, but only if they get written down before the debate ends and never touched afterward. The failure I would watch for is the signpost getting quietly reinterpreted at month six so the thesis survives. Do you store them somewhere the models cannot go back and edit?

replies.author: capibara13
replies.body:
Yep, moving the goalposts via hindsight bias is an easy trap to fall into.   
Luckily, so far most of my long-term investments I made using Rauno have a higher ROI than it initially predicted, as opposed to lower. But yes, moving these signposts afterwards is an interesting concept to give some thought.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: beating your own forecast is the more comfortable failure of the two, but it's still a calibration miss. worth logging the signed error each time rather than just whether it cleared the mark.

replies.author: capibara13
replies.body: Yes that's a great idea for sure.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Cheers. Write the signed error down from the very first forecast, going back and reconstructing it later never actually happens.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
the beating-it direction is the one nobody goes back and audits though. when it lands under, you dig through the reasoning. when it lands over, you just bank it and move on.

so if it is miscalibrated that way you would find out slowly, or not at all.

comments.author: presentofai
comments.body: debate setups have the opposite problem from what youd hope. models cave to each other fast and converge on agreement, so you end up laundering one guess into fake consensus. for a trade thesis thats worse than asking one model and just sitting with the uncertainty.

replies.author: capibara13
replies.body:
To stop them from caving, you have to treat agreement as a failure state in the prompt mechanics:

1. Explicit anti-deference rules: Hard negative constraints like: "Do not validate, summarize, or build upon the previous model's points. Your mandate is exclusively to identify where the preceding logic breaks down, where costs are understated, or where macro variables are missing."
2. Forced counter-mandates: Framing the follow-up models not as conversational peers, but as explicit counter-parties.

If an adversarial model genuinely can't find a structural flaw after being forced to attack it, that tells you something useful. But yes, if you don't explicitly forbid agreement upfront, you 100% end up with laundered confirmation bias. For example, the system prompt in Rauno explicitly frames the session as a fact-based debate where intellectual honesty and stress-testing take priority over consensus.
